extracted.intended_audience: academics who serve on or apply to research funding panels (grant/fellowship applicants and reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative scripts used by panelists to judge research proposals and fellowship applications across humanities, history, and social sciences, covering formal program criteria (significance, methods, theory, feasibility) and informal/evanescent criteria (elegance, intelligence, moral qualities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of topic — Intellectual
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual significance of the research topic (scholarly importance within discipline; contribution to existing literature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists—particularly humanists—emphasize whether the topic speaks to major literatures and whether it addresses what remains to be done; expertise and personal taste shape judgments about whether a topic is ‘‘important.’’ References: ‘‘intellectual signiﬁcance’’ used as a criterion by many panelists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of topic — Political and social
rubrics_metrics.description: Political and social significance of the research topic (relevance to social issues, policy, marginalized groups, or political questions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some panelists (constructivist/utilitarian styles) privilege social relevance: producing instrumental knowledge, giving voice to under-represented groups, policy implications. Others resist instrumentalism and defend 'knowledge for knowledge's sake.' Use of social significance is contested and can raise concerns about advocacy or subjectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of impact — On academia/field/knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Expected impact of findings on academia, the applicant's field, or knowledge more broadly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists more often focus on the project's likely influence on knowledge and on academia than on immediate social/political impact. Distinguish impact on 'academia', 'field', and 'knowledge'—these are referenced separately in panel discussions and influence funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of impact — Political
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential political impact of the research (influencing policy, power relations, distribution of power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some evaluators weigh whether research will affect power distributions or address urgent societal issues; others are skeptical of political impact as a funding criterion and worry about instrumentalization or political bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of impact — Social
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential social impact (practical benefits for communities, marginalized voices, or social problems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associated with utilitarian/constructivist orientations; examples include research aimed at improving people's lives or giving voice to diasporic peoples, women, popular/folk idioms. Use varies by discipline and individual taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemological style — Constructivist
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluative style that privileges research presenting personal, political, and social elements as relevant to research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructivists value research tied to social change, giving voice, interpretive/contextual approaches. They may emphasize reflexivity and the political dimensions of scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemological style — Comprehensive
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluative style that privileges 'knowledge for knowledge's sake' and emphasizes a substantially informed rationale and theoretically informed agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensive style values theoretical grounding, careful articulation of rationale, attention to complexity; majority of panelists invoke this style. It is used across disciplines and focuses on scholarly significance and theoretical contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemological style — Positivist
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluative style that emphasizes generalizing empirical findings, testing hypotheses, disproving theories, and methodological rigor geared toward generalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positivists favor formal models, hypothesis testing, and generalizability; more common among social scientists. They may distrust reflexive or heavily theoretical approaches that lack empirical generalizability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemological style — Utilitarian
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluative style oriented toward solving 'real world' problems and producing instrumental knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utilitarians prize applicability, policy relevance, and practical problem solving. They often treat social significance and policy implications as central evaluative dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulation of theory and data (theory–method alignment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear alignment between the research question, theory, proposed methods, and the evidence mobilized to answer the question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists prize proposals where theory, method, and evidence fit together (described as 'craft at its best'). Strong proposals explain how cases address theory, why cases are selected, and how evidence will resolve the puzzle. Disagreement exists about whether hypotheses must be pre-specified or may emerge inductively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods — appropriateness and rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriateness of methodological choices for the research goal, including responsiveness to methodological concerns and rationale for fieldwork.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs often mention 'responsiveness to methodological concerns' and 'rationale for field work.' Evaluators look for methods suitable to the question and convincing justification of methodological choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper use of theory (integration vs. abuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate, integrated, and reflective use of theory (including reflexivity), as opposed to superficial or abusive deployment of theory/jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humanists value reflexivity and theoretically astute positioning; however, many panelists strongly criticize 'abuse of theory'—jargon, name-dropping, or 'theory using people'—and favor clarity. 'Clarity trumps elegance.' Theory should be used as a tool and integrated with empirical material, not tacked on or used to parade sophistication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility (scope, timeline, preparedness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feasibility of the proposed project: scope, timeline, plan of work, budget, and applicant preparedness (language skills, prior experience, advisers, track record).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: About half of panelists mention feasibility. Evaluators ask if 'the right proposal [is] being done by the right person' and expect a realistic 'road map.' Track record matters but panelists disagree about its proper weight; feasibility also includes human limitations and evidence availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal/'evanescent' criteria — elegance, excitement, cultural capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Less-official qualities that influence judgments: elegance, ability to generate excitement, display of cultural capital; the sense that an applicant is the 'it' person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists commonly appeal to intuition, 'flair', and aesthetic judgments (striking/elegant proposals). These informal criteria are ubiquitous, not merely tiebreakers, and are seen as intrinsic to identifying excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of intelligence (intellectual subtlety and complexity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of intellectual ability shown in subtlety, complexity of framing, clarity and order in presenting complex ideas, and nimbleness of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators look for applicants who can balance conflicting information, present complication clearly, and demonstrate analytical elegance. In elite competitions, finer gradations of intellectual refinement (articulation, nimbleness, listening) are prized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal and moral qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant personal/moral attributes referenced in evaluation: interestingness, excitement, determination, humility, authenticity (and conversely being boring or untrustworthy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists mention these qualities as part of judgments about candidates; they can combine with intellectual factors to define meritorious applicants, especially in interview-based or elite selection contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for generalizability vs. particularized/middle‑level claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which evaluators value broad generalization versus detailed, context-rich, or middle‑level generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economists/purposely positivist reviewers often favor generalization and broad applicability; many historians prefer middle‑level generalizations or well-integrated case studies that illuminate broader issues without overreaching. Disciplinary taste influences how much generalization is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concerns about bias and political influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Awareness of potential bias when factoring social/political significance or track record; concern that political commitments may distort scholarly judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 45% of respondents mention concern with bias. Some worry social relevance leads to subjectivism or advocacy; others point to 'pseudo-neutral' stances that mask political differences. Panelists attempt to balance these concerns with standards and contextualization.
